design_detail: Meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies comparing cognitive test performance between people with methamphetamine use disorder and healthy controls: 44 studies (1592 users, 1820 controls) published before May 2017, pooled by Comprehensive Meta-Analysis v2 in 12 cognitive domains plus a global measure.
can_establish: The average standardized difference between users with a use disorder and healthy controls in the studies available to 2017, by domain, and that small studies with small effects are probably missing from the literature.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the differences (no premorbid data; the education meta-regression cannot answer this); the size of the difference after correcting for publication bias (no adjusted estimate is given); or any effect of abstinence (short abstinence in almost all studies).

sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine use disorder; healthy control group; validated neuropsychological tests; published before 1 May 2017 (p. 155). Excluded: tasks performed in a scanner, HIV-affected samples, users not meeting abuse/dependence criteria, duplicate samples, missing data, no control group, children/adolescents and non-English papers (pp. 155–157; Figure 1).
sample.selection_effects: Only 14 of 27 studies reported abstinence length; weighted mean abstinence 4.5 months (3.3 months excluding one study at 77.4 months) (p. 158).

exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed; listed as an unexamined confounder with route, quantity, duration, depression, alcohol and smoking (pp. 158–159).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Weighted mean 4.5 months in the 14 studies reporting it (p. 158).

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No premorbid cognitive data; education used as a proxy (p. 158).

outcomes.instruments: Validated neuropsychological tests assigned to 12 domains using Lezak et al. (2012) and the group's earlier meta-analyses; consensus of three authors (pp. 155–156).
outcomes.operationalization: Cohen's d, positive = users worse; within-study averaging of tests per domain (p. 156).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni for the four meta-regressions (p. 156); none across domains.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (p. 157), d with 95% CI (users worse): global cognition 0.46 (0.33–0.60, 27 studies); attention 0.43 (0.02–0.84, 4); executive functions 0.49 (0.37–0.61, 27); impulsivity/reward 0.93 (0.72–1.14, 8); language/verbal fluency 0.43 (0.21–0.65, 14); social cognition 1.12 (0.81–1.42, 3); speed of processing 0.34 (0.22–0.45, 19, after excluding one outlier); verbal learning 0.59 (0.40–0.77, 13); verbal memory 0.40 (0.29–0.51, 14); visual learning 0.28 (−0.11 to 0.66, 5; not significant); visual memory 0.47 (0.20–0.75, 7); visuospatial 0.39 (0.13–0.65, 4, after excluding one outlier); working memory 0.51 (0.30–0.72, 15). Publication bias: Egger t=5.1, p=0.00003, on global cognition; no bias-adjusted estimate (p. 156). Meta-regressions on global cognition: age (27 studies, p=0.55), sex ratio (26, p=0.53), education (25, β=0.061, p=0.1), abstinence (14, p=0.61), all non-significant (p. 156).
analysis.selective_reporting: Fixed- or random-effects model chosen per domain from the Q test at p<0.1 (p. 156); domains with 3–8 studies (social cognition, impulsivity) were pooled with fixed effects, where heterogeneity tests have little power.
analysis.power: Low for moderators and small domains (acknowledged pp. 158–159).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Users with a use disorder score on average about half a standard deviation below healthy controls overall, with larger differences on impulsivity/reward tasks (8 studies) and social cognition (3 studies), and strong evidence that small studies with small effects are missing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes moderate impairment and broad deficits (p. 154), which matches the data as associations. Elsewhere the paper calls them deficits induced by chronic methamphetamine use (p. 156) and reads the non-significant education meta-regression as tentatively suggesting the deficits are secondary to use (p. 158), which a null study-level regression on 25 studies cannot show. The highly significant Egger test is described as meaning the deficits are possibly slightly over-estimated (p. 159), without an adjusted estimate to support 'slightly'.

timeline.event: Earlier meta-analysis of 17 studies with similar average differences
Meta-analysis restricted to abstinent samples, with risk-of-bias assessment and prediction intervals: smaller and domain-dependent differences
Non-overlapping meta-analysis of 68 studies from 2017–2025: larger average differences, visuospatial largest rather than spared

replication.where_it_stands: Average differences of roughly half a standard deviation replicate; the domain profile differs between meta-analyses (visuospatial spared here, largest in Cao et al., 2026).

funding.declared_conflicts: The first author is co-principal investigator on a trial funded by Otsuka Pharmaceuticals and holds a grant from Otsuka and the Eli Lilly Canada Chair on schizophrenia research; the other authors declare none (p. 159).
funding.affiliations_note: The alcohol and cocaine meta-analyses used for comparison are by the same group.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant meta-analysis with premorbid ability measures and bias-adjusted pooled estimates; replication of the social-cognition and impulsivity findings in larger samples; longitudinal designs.

domains.note: Five sources and cross-referencing; keywords given; English only.
Consensus between authors; independence of screening not described.
Two extractors named; independence not described.

domains.domain: List of excluded studies with reasons (critical)
Risk of bias of individual studies (critical)

domains.note: Model choice conditioned on a low-power Q test.

domains.domain: Risk of bias considered in interpretation (critical)

domains.note: Egger test and funnel plot; strong asymmetry; no adjusted estimate.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No protocol, no risk-of-bias assessment of included studies and no list of exclusions; the pooled estimates average confounded comparisons and are probably inflated by publication bias.

key_findings.finding: 44 studies, 1592 users and 1820 controls; search of five databases to May 2017.
Global cognition d=0.46 (95% CI 0.33–0.60, 27 studies); executive functions 0.49; verbal learning 0.59; working memory 0.51; speed of processing 0.34; visual learning not significant.
Largest differences on impulsivity/reward tasks (d=0.93, 8 studies) and social cognition (d=1.12, 3 studies).
key_findings.note: Both pooled with fixed effects; social cognition rests on 3 studies.

key_findings.finding: Strong evidence of publication bias on global cognition (Egger t=5.1, p=0.00003); no adjusted estimate reported.
Age, sex ratio, education and abstinence did not significantly moderate global effect sizes (25–27 studies; abstinence 14 studies).
Weighted mean abstinence 4.5 months, or 3.3 months excluding one study; most studies tested people in early abstinence.
Abstinence was not an inclusion criterion, and at least one included study tested people currently using (Simon et al., 2002, by its title), so the pooled estimates mix current and abstinent users.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstinence meta-regression reports β=−0.004 with a 95% CI of −0.17 to 0.01, an interval not consistent with that point estimate (probably a typographical error).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence result cannot be read precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the search identified 5516 records after excluding duplicates; Figure 1 shows 5516 identified and 2764 after duplicates were removed.
A non-significant study-level education regression is read as tentative evidence that deficits are secondary to methamphetamine use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of an ecological association is not evidence of causation.

reporting_issues.issue: Social cognition (3 studies) has Q=4.7, printed as p=0.1; with 2 degrees of freedom the exact p is about 0.095, which meets the paper's own heterogeneity criterion (p<0.1), yet it was pooled with a fixed-effect model (no random-effects footnote in Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: A random-effects model would give a wider interval than 0.81–1.42; the ranking of social cognition as the largest deficit rests on 3 studies and an interval that is too narrow.

reporting_issues.issue: The global estimate pools 27 of the 44 studies (those with two or more domains); the number of participants behind it, or behind any domain estimate, is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The totals of 1592 users and 1820 controls describe all 44 studies, not the global or the domain estimates.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 154–160 (all pages; supplementary table not read)

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: abstinence was not an inclusion criterion; at least one included study is of current users (Simon et al., 2002, per its title, p. 160).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed: the four inclusion criteria (p. 155) do not mention abstinence; the included Simon et al. (2002) is titled as a study of current users (p. 160). Added as a key finding because the claims on lasting deficits cite this meta-analysis.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: social cognition (Q=4.7, df=2, p≈0.095) meets the paper's own criterion for heterogeneity (p<0.1) but was pooled with a fixed-effect model, which narrows its interval (Table 1, p. 157; rule on p. 156).
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed the chi-square p (0.0954). Confirmed the model rule (p. 156) and the absence of the random-effects mark for social cognition in Table 1 (p. 157). Added.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the global estimate (d 0.46) pools 27 of the 44 studies; the number of participants behind it is not reported; the encyclopedia's magnitude line pairs it with 44 studies, 1592 vs 1820.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed (Methods 2.3, p. 156; Table 1, p. 157). Added as a reporting issue so that claims do not attach the 44-study totals to the global estimate.
